disposition.note:
What is Contact Dermatitis?
Contact dermatitis is a skin rash that occurs when your skin comes into contact with something that irritates it or causes an allergic reaction. Common causes include:
Plants (poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac)
Metals (nickel in jewelry, belt buckles, snaps)
Fragrances and preservatives in soaps, lotions, or cosmetics
Cleaning products, detergents, and solvents
Latex or rubber
Certain medications applied to the skin
The rash usually appears as red, itchy skin that may have bumps, blisters, or dry/cracked patches. It typically develops in the area that touched the substance.

Your Treatment Plan

Topical steroid cream or ointment — Apply a thin layer to the affected area as directed (usually 1–2 times daily). Do not use on the face, eyelids, or groin unless specifically instructed by your doctor.
Oral antihistamine (such as cetirizine/Zyrtec or diphenhydramine/Benadryl) — May help relieve itching. Note: diphenhydramine can cause drowsiness.
Oral steroids (such as prednisone) — If the rash covers a large area or is severe, your doctor may prescribe a steroid pill or liquid to be taken by mouth. Take exactly as directed and do not stop early, as the rash can come back.

Skin Care at Home
Identify and avoid the cause. The most important step is figuring out what caused the rash and staying away from it. The rash will not fully clear until contact with the substance stops.
Moisturize frequently. Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer or emollient (such as Vaseline, CeraVe, or Aquaphor) several times a day to help repair and protect the skin barrier.
Cool compresses. Apply a cool, damp cloth to the rash for 15–20 minutes several times a day to soothe itching and inflammation.
Oatmeal baths. A lukewarm bath with colloidal oatmeal can help relieve itching. Avoid hot water, which can worsen the rash.
Wash gently. Use mild, fragrance-free soap. Pat skin dry — do not rub.
Wear soft, loose clothing over the affected area.

Important Do's and Don'ts
Do:
Wash your skin with soap and water as soon as possible after contact with a known irritant or allergen
Wear protective gloves when handling chemicals, cleaning products, or plants
Finish all prescribed medications as directed

Don't:
Do NOT scratch the rash — scratching can break the skin and lead to infection
Do NOT apply the steroid cream more often or longer than prescribed
Do NOT use steroid cream on your face or skin folds unless your doctor specifically told you to
Do NOT use products that contain the substance that caused your rash — read ingredient labels carefully

Pain and Itch Relief
Ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin): 400–600 mg every 6–8 hours as needed with food
Acetaminophen (Tylenol): 500–1,000 mg every 6–8 hours as needed
Calamine lotion may be applied to the rash to help with itching
Antihistamines as described above

When to Call Your Doctor or Go to the ER
Rash is spreading rapidly or covers a large area of your body
Severe swelling, especially of the face, eyes, or lips
Difficulty breathing or swallowing (call 911)
Signs of skin infection: increasing redness, warmth, pus or yellow crusting, red streaks, or fever
Rash does not improve after 2–3 weeks of treatment
Rash keeps coming back despite avoiding the suspected cause
Rash involves your eyes, mouth, or genitals

Follow-Up
If the rash does not improve within 1–2 weeks, return to the clinic for re-evaluation.
If the cause of the rash is unknown or the rash keeps returning, your doctor may refer you for patch testing — a specialized test to identify exactly which substances are causing the allergic reaction.
